findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes
findings.body: Create derives the background legacy-write context from the incoming request context using context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The same pattern is used in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. When the HTTP handler returns, the request context is canceled, so the child context is also canceled even though the legacy write is intended to continue asynchronously. This can abort legacy writes immediately after the API response is sent, defeating mode 3's dual-write safety behavior and causing divergence between unified storage and legacy storage. Use a detached context such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx), or a dedicated background context that preserves values but not cancellation.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are unordered and untracked
findings.body: Each write path launches an independent goroutine to create, update, delete, or delete-collection in legacy storage. There is no ordering, queue, mutex, wait group, or lifecycle tracking. Concurrent operations on the same object may complete in legacy storage in a different order than they were applied to unified storage, for example a delete arriving before a create or an old update arriving after a newer update. This can leave legacy storage inconsistent with unified storage. Destroy may also run while these goroutines are still active. If legacy writes are meant to be a safe fallback, they should be serialized per object or managed by a tracked background worker.

findings.title: Background legacy-write goroutines do not recover from panics
findings.body: The asynchronous legacy write paths use bare goroutines without panic recovery. Because legacy writes are secondary and best-effort in mode 3, a panic in legacy storage code or serialization should not crash the whole API server process. Add a deferred recover in these goroutines and log/metric the failure.

findings.title: Legacy update is performed with the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage
findings.body: After Storage.Update succeeds, the code asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will re-evaluate UpdatedObject against the legacy store's current object, which may produce a different result than the update that was applied in unified storage, especially for patches, defaults, generated fields, or resourceVersion handling. Mode 3 treats unified storage as the source of truth, so legacy should receive the final object returned by Storage.Update. The previous implementation wrapped the updated object for the legacy call; removing that wrapper creates a real risk of silent divergence between unified storage and legacy storage.

findings.title: Legacy create uses the original request object instead of the created object
findings.body: After Storage.Create succeeds, the asynchronous Legacy.Create call is made with the original obj rather than the created object returned by unified storage. If unified storage assigns a name, UID, creation timestamp, defaults, or otherwise changes the object, legacy storage may create a different object identity or fail validation. To mirror unified storage, the legacy create should use the created object's identity and spec, clearing any fields that are invalid on create such as resourceVersion if needed.

findings.title: Storage Delete errors, including NotFound, prevent legacy cleanup
findings.body: Delete returns immediately when Storage.Delete fails, so Legacy.Delete is never attempted. The previous implementation treated NotFound specially and still attempted deletion from legacy storage. If an object exists only in legacy storage, or remains there after unified storage no longer has it, this change can leave stale legacy data that may reappear if the dual-writer mode changes. The same issue exists for DeleteCollection, where any storage error skips legacy cleanup. At minimum, NotFound from unified storage should still trigger legacy deletion.

findings.title: Delete storage duration metric uses object name as kind label
findings.body: In Delete, the success path records storage duration with name as the third argument: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Other methods pass options.Kind for that label. This puts the resource name into the kind metric label, producing incorrect metrics and potentially high-cardinality series, breaking dashboards or alerts that aggregate by kind. It should pass options.Kind.

findings.title: Storage create failures are recorded as legacy duration
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Operators relying on dual-writer metrics will see false legacy errors and missing storage errors. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation.

findings.title: Storage update failures are recorded as legacy duration
findings.body: When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation so mode 3 metrics correctly distinguish unified storage failures from legacy failures.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection failure is recorded as storage duration
findings.body: In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the error from d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration. This misattributes legacy latency and errors to unified storage. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy operation.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: In Create, errors from Legacy.Create are only reflected in a metric. The same applies to the asynchronous legacy operations in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Since mode 3 writes to legacy storage as a safety measure, silent failures make it difficult to diagnose divergence. Log the error with the object kind, name or identifier, and operation before recording the metric.

findings.title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched logger
findings.body: Delete creates log := d.Log.WithValues(...), but then sets ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the added values for downstream logging. Any code that uses klog.FromContext(ctx) inside Storage.Delete or Legacy.Delete will miss the name, kind, and method fields. It should use ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not wait for or verify asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: TestMode3_Create calls dw.Create and returns immediately, but the legacy create happens in a goroutine. The tests do not synchronize with that goroutine, do not assert that legacy methods were actually called, and use a shared mock for both legacy and unified storage, so calls to either store are indistinguishable. As a result, the tests can pass even if asynchronous legacy writes are skipped, canceled, reordered, or otherwise broken. Similar gaps exist for Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Add synchronization and explicit assertions that legacy storage receives the expected calls.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The added mode 3 scenarios run doPlaylistTests, which performs create/update/delete operations through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the change. This makes the integration test flaky and also masks eventual-consistency behavior. The test should poll or otherwise wait for legacy convergence, or mode 3 tests should use a synchronous/test-only legacy write path.
